snip.t: A bedside culture report for a patient with deep osteomyelitis grows *Staphylococcus aureus* that is sensitive to oxacillin, cefazolin, erythromycin, and vancomycin.

Infection risk: Anemia of chronic disease or marrow suppression impairs neutrophil function; iron overload favours bacterial growth. — Sepsis, osteomyelitis, invasive fungal disease. — Higher morbidity; early antimicrobial coverage essential.
Metastatic infection: Septic arthritis, vertebral osteomyelitis — Localised back pain, joint effusion
Other: Pneumonia, osteomyelitis, chorioamnionitis (in pregnancy), relapsing fever.
| Sickle‑cell vaso‑occlusive crisis with infection | Known sickle cell, bone pain, fever, splenic sequestration | Positive sickle‑cell screen, pain pattern, possible osteomyelitis on imaging |
Sickle cell disease: Leg ulcers, osteomyelitis — Vaso‑occlusive crises, poor perfusion
Bone tenderness / swelling: Vaso‑occlusion in marrow causing infarction; may progress to osteomyelitis (especially Salmonella).
| Osteomyelitis (Salmonella) | Localized bone pain, fever, elevated ESR/CRP | Positive bone culture, MRI shows sequestrum |

ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Osteomyelitis is infection of bone and marrow that can be acute or chronic. Prompt diagnosis, appropriate antibiotics and surgical debridement are essential to prevent permanent damage and systemic complications.

sections.p: Infection of bone tissue, usually bacterial, confirmed by imaging and microbiology. Diagnosis requires clinical suspicion, elevated inflammatory markers, and evidence of bone involvement on MRI or bone scan.
b: Acute: symptoms <2 weeks, often hematogenous.
Chronic: >6 weeks, may have sinus tract.

t.b: Does the bone show edema or abscess? Positive MRI confirms osteomyelitis and guides surgery.
Is a pathogen present in the bloodstream? Positive culture identifies organism for targeted therapy.
What organism is in the infected bone? Provides definitive microbiology when blood cultures are negative.

sections.p: Use the Cierny‑Mader classification: anatomic type (I‑IV) and physiologic class (A‑C). This guides need for surgery versus medical therapy alone.
b: Type I: medullary infection only.
Type II: superficial cortical involvement.
Type III: localized full‑thickness cortical disease.
Type IV: diffuse disease affecting the whole bone.

sections.p: Most cases are bacterial, with Staphylococcus aureus leading. In low‑resource settings, consider Mycobacterium tuberculosis, Gram‑negative bacilli, and fungal agents.
b: Hematogenous spread (children, S. aureus).
Contiguous spread from soft‑tissue infection or trauma.
Direct inoculation after surgery or penetrating injury.
Chronic TB osteomyelitis in endemic regions.

sections.p: Pain is the hallmark, often deep and worsening at night. Swelling, warmth, and fever may be present. Chronic disease can produce a draining sinus tract.
b: Acute: rapid onset pain, fever, leukocytosis.
Chronic: persistent pain, sinus, low‑grade fever, weight loss.

sections.p: Combine laboratory, imaging and microbiology to confirm infection, stage disease and plan treatment.
b: ESR/CRP: track inflammation.
Plain X‑ray: late changes (sequestrum, involucrum).

t.b: Is there systemic inflammation? Elevated values support infection but are nonspecific.
Are there bone lysis or new bone formation? Positive after 2‑3 weeks; helps assess chronic changes.
Is cortical destruction present? Useful when MRI unavailable.

sections.p: Unchecked infection can lead to sepsis, pathological fracture, growth‑plate arrest in children, and chronic draining sinuses that cause amyloidosis.
b: Rapidly expanding swelling.
Unexplained hypotension or tachycardia.
New neurologic deficit near spine.

sections.p: Treat the pathogen, remove necrotic bone, and support healing. Antibiotics are given intravenously initially, then orally, guided by culture.
b: Empiric IV anti‑staphylococcal (e.g., cefazolin) pending cultures.
Add MRSA coverage (vancomycin) if risk factors present.
For TB, start standard anti‑TB regimen.
Surgical debridement to excise sequestrum and allow drainage.

sections.p: Monitor inflammatory markers, wound healing and functional recovery. Vaccination, wound care and early treatment of skin infections reduce recurrence.
b: Repeat ESR/CRP at 2‑week intervals until normal.
Serial imaging if clinical response is poor.
Educate patients on foot hygiene in diabetics.

sections.p: Conditions that mimic bone infection must be considered.
b: Bone tumor (pain, swelling, elevated ESR).
Septic arthritis (joint pain, effusion).
Chronic osteitis from sickle‑cell vaso‑occlusion.

sections.p: Some tests may be falsely normal or abnormal, leading to delayed diagnosis.
b: Normal X‑ray early in acute disease.
Low CRP in immunocompromised patients.
Negative blood cultures in chronic TB osteomyelitis.

whenToSeekHelp: High fever with chills and worsening pain
Signs of sepsis (low blood pressure, fast heart rate)

faq.q: Why is MRI preferred for early osteomyelitis?
faq.a: It shows bone marrow edema before X‑ray changes and helps locate abscesses.

faq.q: When is oral antibiotic therapy appropriate?
faq.a: After 2‑4 weeks of IV therapy with clinical improvement and a susceptible organism.
Mild acute cases may respond to antibiotics alone, but necrotic bone usually requires debridement.

exam: Describe the Cierny‑Mader classification and its clinical relevance.
List the first‑line empiric antibiotics for acute pyogenic osteomyelitis in a patient without MRSA risk.
Explain how a draining sinus tract indicates chronic osteomyelitis and its potential systemic complications.
